newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mining agency finds undersea metal deposit.
newsitem.headline: Japan mining agency finds undersea metal deposit.

text.p: Japan's Metal Mining Agency said on Tuesday it had discovered a high-grade undersea metal deposit in Japanese territorial waters west of Okinawa.
Sulfide ore mounds were found over an area 600 by 1,100 metres in the Okinawa Trough at a depth of about 1,600 metres in a government-funded programme to explore the seabed.
Ten samples were graded at an average of 5.2 grams of gold per tonne, 449.5 grams of silver, 0.49 percent copper, 4.07 percent lead and 7.70 percent zinc.

In 1995, the agency began a 10-year programme, budgeted at 200 million to 300 million yen per year, to explore the Okinawa Trough for hydrothermal deposits, which form around undersea hot springs that release water at temperatures above 200 degrees Celsius.

Toshio Sakasegawa of the agency's technology development section acknowledged that exploitation of hydrothermal mounds may be more difficult than for manganese nodules, which can be plucked from the seabed floor.
He added that, while experimental recovery and environmental impact studies had already been carried out for manganese nodules, such work had yet to be done on hydrothermal deposits.

While the potential commercial exploitation of hydrothermal deposits was still far off in the future, he said, some recovery methods under review included the use of robots to dig up the ore or the construction of a container around the deposit, which would be filled with fluid to leech the minerals into a solution that could be drawn to the surface.
